title: The chain (Avot 1:1)
hook: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on: Joshua, elders, prophets, the Great Assembly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pirkei Avot: the Mishnah's little book of sayings, read on summer afternoons. Your line was wisdom in small sayings. Did you carry one sentence all day? Today, we open it to the very first line. Day two hundred thirty-three.

Think about how you learned to make your family's best dish. Probably not from a cookbook. Somebody showed you. And they learned it from somebody who showed them. If you traced it back, you'd find a line of hands, each passing it to the next, adjusting a little, keeping the heart of it. Most books of wisdom open with the wisdom. This one doesn't. Before a single piece of advice, Pirkei Avot stops to answer a question: where did this come from? Who handed it to whom? Today: the chain.
screen: `THE FAMILY RECIPE.` → `A LINE OF HANDS.` → `WHERE DID THIS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Avot, in paraphrase. Moses received Torah from Sinai, and handed it to Joshua. Joshua handed it to the elders. The elders to the prophets. And the prophets handed it to the men of the Great Assembly. That's it. A list of hands. Two Hebrew verbs carry the whole thing. Kibbel: he received. And masar: he handed over. Kibbel is the root of the word kabbalah, which at first simply meant tradition: what's been received. Masar gives us masorah, the passing down. Notice a few things the rabbis noticed. It says Moses received Torah, without the word the. Many commentators say that's on purpose: not just the written scroll, but the teaching, the explanations, the way to live it. The oral part, which you can only get from a person. And every link is a person. Joshua, Moses's student. The elders who led after him. The prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest. And the Great Assembly, which tradition says gathered in Ezra's time, after the exile in Babylon. By the end of this chapter, the chain will run all the way down to named rabbis, teacher after teacher. And there's a reason Avot begins here. Everything that follows, be patient, be kind, find a teacher, isn't one clever person's opinion. It arrived through hands. Which means that the day you teach anyone anything, you're a link too.
screen: `MOSES RECEIVED TORAH FROM SINAI.` · `KIBBEL AND MASAR.` · `JOSHUA, ELDERS, PROPHETS, ASSEMBLY.` · `EVERY LINK IS A PERSON.` · then, large: `HANDED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank one of your teachers. Settle, and breathe. Think back to someone who handed you something that stuck. Not always a classroom teacher. A boss, an aunt, an older kid on the bus, a coach who told you the truth. Picture them. What did they hand you? Now trace it one link back: who do you think handed it to them? Hold both of them for a moment, gratefully. The bell holds the time.
The chain. Avot's first line: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on, hand to hand, to Joshua, the elders, the prophets and the Great Assembly.
Your line: handed down. Today, send a short thank-you to one person who taught you something, and tell them what it was. Day two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish learning is traditionally passed from teacher to student, and many Jews cite a teaching in the name of the person they learned it from, a practice Avot itself praises.

fork.setup: you're opening a book of wisdom for the ages. what goes on the first page?
options: the most important piece of advice.
a list of who handed the teaching to whom.
a warning to take it seriously.
fork.reveal: Avot opens with the chain: Moses to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets, to the Great Assembly. the advice comes after.

original.note: Hebrew: he handed over. The verb of the chain in Avot 1:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of old names.
what it means: the teaching arrived hand to hand, each link a person, and now includes anyone who teaches.
what a scholar hears: kibbel and masar give Hebrew the words kabbalah, tradition received, and masorah, tradition handed down.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 6:6 (saying a thing in the name of the one who said it)

notes: Avot 1:1 paraphrased; no public-domain translation is quoted.
'Torah' without the definite article read as including Oral Torah: common commentary (e.g. Bartenura and others); confirm.
Kabbalah's early meaning as 'received tradition' and masorah from m-s-r: confirm etymology phrasing.
The Great Assembly in Ezra's era is traditional dating.
howItsDone cites Avot 6:6 on quoting teachings in the name of their author; confirm.
